title: Components and interaction
instruction: Build controls that work by keyboard and screen reader and announce every change.
intro: A component is a part of a page that a reader works, such as a button, a menu or a search field. Each rule here gives one component as code to copy, drawn live in the light theme on Newsprint and in the dark theme on Charcoal, and a table of its states, its keys, its name, its target size and what a screen reader hears when it changes.

The code reads only tokens.css, the file that holds every color, size and type style as a named value, so one copy follows either theme. A screen reader hears the name, role, state and status line the code hands it, and each screen reader words these its own way. How each state looks and moves comes from chapter 17.

groups.title: Actions and choices
groups.line: Buttons act on the page. Toggles, choices and the theme switch hold a state the reader sets, which a screen reader can name.

groups.title: Moving around
groups.line: Links take a reader somewhere, and the masthead and the location lists show where the reader is now.

groups.title: Showing and hiding
groups.line: A disclosure opens a part of the page in place, and tabs switch between views of one thing.

groups.title: Tables, code and files
groups.line: Tables sort where they stand and wide content scrolls inside its own frame. The copy and download controls say in words what they did.

groups.title: Finding and filling in
groups.line: Search, filters and forms tell the reader what they found or what to fix, in a status line or beside the field.

groups.title: Messages and waiting
groups.line: Each message carries its mark and its first word, and a part that waits for data says what is coming or what is missing.

groups.title: Records, readers and drawings
groups.line: The controls our civic records and atlas drawings need: the live tracker, the report reader, the loop stepper, the controls on a drawing and the typed ID chip.

rules.title: Use a button to act on the page, and keep an unavailable one in reach with its reason.
rule: A button acts on the page: it sends a form, copies a value or starts a loop. A control that takes the reader to another page or place is a link (Rule 18.5). A view has one primary button at most, Charcoal on Newsprint and Newsprint on Charcoal. The ask, the Pillar Red button for the one way to take part, appears only where Rule 05.3 gives the view its working red, and every other button is quiet: its word in ink inside a 1 px edge. A utility icon sits beside the word (Rule 11.11).

When an action cannot run yet, its button stays in place and keeps its focus. It carries aria-disabled, draws a dashed edge and points to a line under it that says why and what makes it work, such as “Fill in your email to send.” While a send runs, its word reads “Sending” and a second press does nothing. While an error on the page holds the red, the ask steps down to the primary look (Rule 11.16).

text: A native button gives every reader the Tab key, Enter, Space and the role “button” with no script. The disabled attribute would take the button out of the Tab order and hide its reason with it, so an unavailable button carries aria-disabled, which keeps both in reach. An underline on hover and a dashed edge when unavailable carry each state in a shape as well as a color.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1, 2.1.1, 2.5.8 and 4.1.2; APG Button pattern

correct.caption: The parts of a button: its word, the 24 px utility icon beside it, its fill or 1 px edge, the 44 px height, the focus ring at its gap, and the reason line an unavailable button points to.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 18.1. Send is grayed out with the disabled attribute and no words, so the Tab key skips it and nobody learns that the email is missing. Its word measures 1.83 to 1 on Newsprint.

rules.title: Turn a setting on or off with a toggle button, and mark it on with a check, bold words and a 2 px edge.
rule: A toggle button turns one thing on or off and keeps its word in both states, such as “Show sources”. A filter chip is a toggle that narrows a list, and chips combine, so a reader can turn on several at once. Each carries aria-pressed, true while it is on.

On looks the same in every product (Rule 17.10): a check before the word, the word in bold and a 2 px edge. Off keeps a 1 px edge and no check. The word stays the same when the state changes, because the check and the pressed state already say it, and a word that flipped would leave a screen reader saying two things at once.

text: A reader learns one look for on and meets it on every chip and toggle. The check and the edge are shapes, so they hold in gray print and in a contrast theme, where a fill drops out, and aria-pressed lets a screen reader say on or off.

rules.title: Offer one of a few choices as radio buttons in a named group.
rule: When a reader picks one of two to five choices and only one can hold, such as the size of a page, use native radio buttons in a fieldset whose legend names the choice. Draw them as a row of segments or as a list, and make the whole segment the label, so a press anywhere on it chooses.

The checked choice takes the one look for a current choice (Rule 17.10): a check before the word, the word in bold and a 2 px edge. A choice applies at once, with no Apply button, and focus stays on it. A choice that cannot be made yet stays in view as a disabled radio, with a line under the row that says why, and the group points to that line with aria-describedby, so a screen reader hears it on entering the group.

text: Radio buttons tell a screen reader that only one choice holds and how many there are, and the arrow keys move between them with no script. A pair of pressed buttons says neither. The arrow keys pass a disabled radio, so the line the group points to tells every reader why it waits.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.3.1, 3.2.2 and 4.1.2; APG Radio Group pattern

failure.caption: Fails Rule 18.3. Nothing names the choice, and the chosen size differs only by its fill. A screen reader hears “Full size” with no group, and a contrast theme loses the fill.

rules.title: Let the reader choose Light, Dark or Match my device, and remember the choice.
rule: Every screen product follows the reader’s device at first and offers a theme switch in the same place on every page, in the masthead or at the top of the phone menu. The switch is a choice (Rule 18.3) of three radio buttons under the legend “Theme”: Light, Dark and Match my device, with Match my device checked until the reader picks another. Each choice is a word, since a sun or a moon does not say which theme is on.

A choice changes the colors at once, with no motion, and focus stays on it. Light and Dark set data-oa-theme on the page’s root and store the choice under the key oa-theme; Match my device removes the key, and the page follows the device again. The script reads and writes the key inside try and catch, so a browser that refuses storage still switches for the visit. A short script in the head applies a stored choice before the first paint (Rule 26.6).

text: Following the device first gives most readers the right theme with no step at all. Three choices keep a way back to the device, which a two-state switch loses once it is pressed. Radio buttons say which theme is on and how many there are, and storage that fails costs the reader only the memory of the choice.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 SC 3.2.3 and 4.1.2; APG Radio Group pattern; design judgment

correct.caption: The parts of the theme switch: the legend “Theme”, the three segments Light, Dark and Match my device, the checked segment’s check, bold word and 2 px edge, and its place in the masthead.

rules.title: Underline every link in text, and say in its name when it leaves our site.
rule: A link takes the reader to another page or place, and its words name the place, such as “the committee’s hearing schedule”. A link in running text keeps a 1 px underline that thickens to 2 px on hover, so its color is never the only sign. A link to another site opens in the same tab; its 16 px mark follows its last word, and the words “(another site)” end its name for screen readers (Rule 11.13).

A skip link is the first stop on every page and shows when it takes focus. A link to the page or place the reader is on carries aria-current and the current look of Rule 18.7. A link to something not built yet stays plain text in the secondary color, with the words “Coming later.”

text: An underline marks a link in gray print, in a contrast theme and for a reader who cannot tell Prussian from Charcoal, which measure 1.41 to 1 against each other. Words that name the place let a reader choose from a list of links read out of their sentences, and a skip link lets a keyboard reader pass the masthead in one press.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1, 2.4.1, 2.4.4 and 3.2.5; APG Link pattern

rules.title: Give every page one masthead, with its parts in a named navigation and a phone menu that holds focus.
rule: The masthead holds the product’s name, which links home, and its parts in a navigation landmark named for what it holds, such as “Parts of the site”. The link to the part the reader is in carries aria-current="page", bold words and a 2 px underline. When the parts no longer fit on one line, they move behind a Menu button, its three bars beside the word Menu, which opens them in a native modal dialog.

The open menu covers the page and holds focus. Focus moves to the current part’s link, the Tab key reaches nothing on the page behind it, and Escape or “Close the menu” shuts it and returns focus to Menu. The rows inside open and close as disclosures (Rule 18.8). A masthead that sticks to the top of the page sets scroll-padding-top to its own height, so no focused element hides under it.

text: One masthead in one place on every page lets a reader find the parts without searching, and a named navigation lets a screen reader jump straight to it. The native dialog makes the page behind it inert, so neither the Tab key nor a screen reader’s reading keys reach a link the menu covers.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.1.2, 2.4.1, 2.4.3, 2.4.11 and 3.2.3; APG Dialog (Modal) pattern and Disclosure Navigation Menu example

rules.title: Show where the reader is with aria-current and a mark that holds without color.
rule: A list of places in a product, such as a chapter rail, an “In this chapter” list or a breadcrumb, marks the reader’s place in two ways at once. The link carries aria-current: “page” for the page itself, “location” for a part of a long page and “step” for a step in a process. A list beside the text marks it with the selected band, a 4 px bar at its left edge and bold words. A short list in a line, such as a breadcrumb, ends on the current page as a link in bold words, with aria-current and no underline, after the links to the places before it.

A list that follows the reader down a long page moves its mark as each part comes into view, and leaves focus and its own scroll where they are. A breadcrumb sits in a navigation landmark named “Breadcrumb”, with its places in an ordered list and the current page last.

text: aria-current lets a screen reader say where the reader is, and the bar and the bold words say it to everyone else in shapes that hold in gray print and in a contrast theme. A mark that follows the scroll helps only while it leaves focus alone.

rules.title: Open a part of the page in place with a disclosure whose words name it and whose chevron turns.
rule: A disclosure shows or hides one part of the page in place, such as a drawing’s lines in words or the sources of a claim. Build it on native details and summary, or on a button with aria-expanded and aria-controls where the part must sit apart from its control. Its words name what opens, such as “The lines in words”, and its chevron points down while it is closed and up while it is open.

The chevron turns within 200 ms where motion is allowed, and at once under reduced motion (Rule 17.4). Opening one disclosure leaves the others as they are, and a printed page opens them all. A stack of disclosures under headings is an accordion, with each summary inside its heading.

text: The native element gives Enter, Space, the expanded state and the open part with no script. A chevron that turns tells a sighted reader what the expanded state tells a screen reader, and words that name the part let a reader decide before opening it.

rules.title: Switch between views of one thing with tabs that move by the arrow keys.
rule: Use tabs only where a reader switches between views of one thing that never need to show at once, such as a drawing, its lines in words and its table. A process with steps takes a stepper (Rule 18.22), and other pages take links. The tabs sit in a tab list named for the thing, each tab names its view, and the selected tab carries aria-selected, a 4 px bar under its word and bold words.

Tab enters the tab list at the selected tab and leaves it for the panel. The arrow keys move between tabs and show each view as it takes focus, and Home and End reach the first and the last. A panel with nothing focusable inside takes tabindex="0", so the Tab key can reach its words.

text: One Tab stop for the whole list keeps a keyboard reader from passing every tab to reach the content, and the roles let a screen reader say which tab holds and how many there are. The bar and the bold words carry the selection in gray print and in a contrast theme.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.3.1, 2.1.1, 2.4.3 and 4.1.2; APG Tabs pattern

correct.caption: The parts of tabs: the tab list and its label, each tab’s words, the selected tab’s 4 px bar and bold words, the focus ring and the panel.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 18.9. The selected view differs only by its fill, every tab is a Tab stop of its own, and the arrow keys do nothing.

rules.title: Build a table from table markup, and sort a column with a button in its heading.
rule: A table has a caption that names it, column headings in th with scope="col", and row headings where the first column names each row. A column a reader can sort holds a button in its heading, with the heading’s words and the 16 px sort arrow after them. The sorted column’s heading carries aria-sort, and the arrow turns up for ascending and down for descending.

A press sorts the column, a second press reverses it, and focus stays on the button. A status line under the table says the order in words, such as “Sorted by date, newest first.” The same line says when rows are loading, what is missing when there are none, and the error with its mark when they fail to load (Rules 18.18 and 18.19). On a phone a table either scrolls inside a scroll region (Rule 18.11) or reads as one card for each row, each value under its column’s word. A table drawn as cards states its roles with role attributes, so it keeps its meaning however CSS displays it.

text: Table markup lets a screen reader name the row and the column of every cell as a reader moves through it. A button in the heading gives sorting a key and a name, and aria-sort with the status line says the new order to a reader who cannot see the arrow turn.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.3.1, 2.1.1, 4.1.2 and 4.1.3; APG Table pattern and its Sortable Table example

correct.caption: The parts of a sortable table: the caption, the column headings, a sort button with its words and 16 px arrow, the sorted heading, the row rules and the status line under the table.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 18.10. The headings are plain cells that only a pointer can sort, and nothing says the order changed.

code.name: Sortable table

specs.value: Each sort button at least 44 px tall, as wide as its words and arrow.

specs.label: Forced colors
specs.value: The arrow draws in currentColor, and the rules between rows hold as borders.

rules.title: Let wide content scroll inside a named frame that the Tab key reaches only while it scrolls.
rule: Content wider than its column, such as a wide table or a drawing at true size, scrolls sideways inside its own frame, so the page itself never scrolls sideways (Rule 07.6). While it overflows, the frame takes tabindex="0" and the role of a group named for what it holds, and the hint “Wider than this column. Scroll the frame sideways to see all of it.” shows above it and describes it. Once it fits, the frame drops all three.
Its focus ring sits inside the frame, where the frame’s edge cannot clip it. The arrow keys scroll a focused frame, and the page around it stays where it is.

text: A keyboard reader can scroll only what takes focus, and a frame that takes focus while it has nothing to scroll is a stop that does nothing. The hint tells a sighted reader the frame holds more, and the name tells a screen reader.

correct.caption: The parts of a scroll region: the frame and its edge, the wide content inside, the hint above it, and the focus ring drawn inside the frame.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 18.11. The table is cut off at the frame’s edge, and no key or hint lets a reader see the columns past it.

code.name: Scroll region

specs.label: States
specs.value: Fits: no Tab stop and no hint. Overflows: the Tab stop, the hint and the name. Focus: the ring inside the frame.

specs.label: Keyboard

specs.label: Accessible name
specs.value: What it holds, such as “The six steps of a bill”, with the hint as its description.

rules.title: Show code in labeled panels, each with a Copy button named for what it copies.
rule: Code a reader can copy sits in one panel per file, HTML, CSS or Script, each with its label and a Copy button named for its panel: “Copy the HTML”, “Copy the CSS” and “Copy the script”. One status line under the panels says what was copied, with the success mark, such as “Copied the CSS, 2 lines, to the clipboard.” The code keeps its own line breaks at 14 px, and a panel that overflows scrolls as Rule 18.11 sets.

When the browser refuses to copy, the line turns into an error with its mark, “Error:”, the Error Band and the 4 px red bar, and says how to copy by hand. The code is then selected in a field under the line, with focus on it (Rule 18.13).

text: A button for each panel says which file a press takes, and a status line says what happened in words, which a screen reader hears while focus stays on the button. A browser can refuse the clipboard, so the refusal leaves the code ready to copy by hand.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.6, 3.3.1 and 4.1.3; APG Button pattern; WAI-ARIA 1.2 status role

correct.caption: The parts of a code block: each panel’s label, its Copy button, the code at 14 px, the status line with the success mark, and the error line with its mark, band and bar over the selected code.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 18.12. After a press the copy icon turns into a check, and no words say what was copied or whether it worked.

code.name: Code block
code.caption: A code block with two panels, live. Press a Copy button and read the line under the panels.

specs.value: APG Button for each Copy; a status line with role="status"; Rule 18.11 for a panel that scrolls.

specs.label: States

specs.label: Keyboard

rules.title: Copy one value with a button that names it, and say the result in words.
rule: A value a builder needs, such as a token’s name or a hex color, sits beside a Copy button. Its visible word is “Copy”, and its name goes on with the value from hidden words, “Copy --oa-color-surface-charcoal”, so every Copy in a table names its own value. The icon’s two sheets stay as drawn after a press (Rule 11.12), and the status line says what happened with the success mark: “Copied --oa-color-surface-charcoal.”

When the browser refuses, the line gives the error with its mark and “Error:”, selects the value in a field and moves focus there, so the reader can copy it by hand with Control and C, or Command and C.

text: A reader who hears “Copy” ten times down a table cannot tell the buttons apart, so each name carries its value. Words in a status line reach a screen reader, where a check that replaces the icon says nothing and looks like a choice someone made.

correct.caption: The parts of a copy control: the value, the Copy button with its two-sheet icon and word, the hidden words that finish its name, and the status line with the success mark.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 18.13. Copy is a 16 px icon with no word, under the 24 px a target needs, and every one in the list has the same name.

specs.label: Keyboard
specs.value: Tab reaches it; Enter or Space copies. Focus stays on it, or moves to the selected value when the browser refuses.

specs.label: Accessible name
specs.value: “Copy” and the value, such as “Copy --oa-color-surface-charcoal”, starting with the visible word.

specs.label: A screen reader hears

specs.label: Target

rules.title: Name each download for its file, type and size, and say why one is not ready.
rule: A download is a link with the download attribute when it fetches a file, and a button when a script builds the file. Its words start with “Download” and name the file, its type and its size, in kilobytes of 1,000 bytes: “Download tokens.css, CSS, 93 KB”. The download icon, an arrow into a tray, sits before the word (Rule 11.11).
A file that is not ready keeps its control in place and in the Tab order, with aria-disabled, a dashed edge and a line that says why and when it will be ready. A press does nothing, and focus stays.

text: The file’s name, type and size let a reader on a slow or metered connection decide before the download starts, and a screen reader reading a list of links hears which file each one fetches. A control that hides until its file is ready leaves a reader wondering whether the file exists.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.4 and 4.1.2; APG Link pattern; design judgment

correct.caption: The parts of a download: the icon before the word, the words from “Download” to the size, the 44 px height, and a file not ready with its dashed edge and reason.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 18.14. Three links all read “Download”, with no file, type or size, so a screen reader’s list of links hears the same word three times.

rules.title: Search with a labeled field that says the count and the advice in one status line.
rule: On a product page a search sits in a search landmark, the search element, so a screen reader can jump straight to it. It has a visible label above its field and a field of type search; a placeholder never stands in for the label. Results update as the reader types, and focus stays in the field. The status line under it gives the count and, when nothing matches, the advice in the same line: “0 of 125 symbols. No symbol matches. Clear the search or the filters to see more.”

Once the field holds text, a Clear the search control appears at its end, a 44 by 44 px cross (Rule 11.11), which empties the field and returns focus to it. Escape does the same. Where results come from a server, the line says “Searching” while they load.

text: A placeholder vanishes at the first letter typed, so the label sits above the field, where it stays in view. A status line lets a screen reader hear the count while focus stays in the field, and advice in the same line tells a reader who found nothing what to do next.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.3.1, 2.4.6, 3.3.2 and 4.1.3; APG Landmarks pattern

correct.caption: The parts of a search: the label, the field and its edge on the field ground, the Clear the search cross once text is in, and the status line with the count and the advice.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 18.15. A placeholder is the only label, at 2.58 to 1, and it disappears once the reader types. The count under the field changes without being said.

rules.title: Put the filters behind one Filters button that says how many are on.
rule: A filter bar narrows a list. Its Filters button, with the funnel beside its word, opens and closes the filters as a disclosure (Rule 18.8), and its name counts what is on: “Filters, 2 on”. Inside, each filter is a chip (Rule 18.2), or a checkbox in a longer form. Every change updates the list at once, and the shared status line with it, such as “12 of 48 bills.”
Clear filters shows only while a filter is on. A press turns every filter off, hides the control and moves focus to Filters, since focus cannot stay on a control that has gone.

text: A count in the name tells a reader who closed the filters that the list is still narrowed. Moving focus to Filters keeps a keyboard reader in place when Clear filters goes, where focus would otherwise fall to the top of the page.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.3, 4.1.2 and 4.1.3; APG Disclosure and Button patterns

correct.caption: The parts of a filter bar: the Filters button with its funnel, word, count and chevron, the chips inside, Clear filters, and the shared status line.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 18.16. The filters open only while a pointer rests on Filters, and its name never says how many are on.

code.caption: A filter bar over a short list, live. Open Filters, turn a chip on, then press Clear filters and see where focus goes.

specs.value: As Rule 18.2.

rules.title: Label every field, point it to its error, and move focus to the first field to fix.
rule: Each field has a visible label above it and, where it helps, a hint under the label joined by aria-describedby, such as “Five digits”. A placeholder never stands in for either. Personal fields carry autocomplete, such as email and postal-code, so the browser can fill them. A field stays open to typing at all times; a Send button that cannot run yet keeps focus and says why, as Rule 18.1 sets.

On a send with mistakes, each wrong field takes aria-invalid, the 4 px Pillar Red bar at its left edge and a message under it joined by aria-describedby: the error mark in ink, “Error:” and how to fix it, on the Error Band on Newsprint and on the ground on Charcoal. Focus moves to the first field to fix, and the ask steps down to the primary look while the error holds the red (Rule 11.16). A send that works writes its result to a status line with the success mark.

text: A label that stays in view helps a reader check what they typed, and autocomplete saves typing for a reader with limited movement. Moving focus to the first field to fix puts the reader where the work is, and the field’s description reads the message there, so nothing needs an alert that interrupts.

correct.caption: The parts of a form field: the label, the hint, the field and its edge on the field ground, and in error, the 4 px red bar, the mark, “Error:” and the fix on the band; then the send button and the success line.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 18.17. The errors sit in a box at the top that names no field, the fields have placeholders in place of labels, and focus stays on Send.

specs.value: the autocomplete attribute: Chrome 14, Edge 12, Firefox 4, Safari 6, Safari on iOS 6.

rules.title: Give every message its mark and its first word, and announce only what changes.
rule: An error, a warning and a success each start with their mark and their words (Rule 11.15). An error starts “Error:” and says how to fix it, beside a 4 px Pillar Red bar. A warning starts “Warning:” beside a 4 px bar in ink, and a success says what happened beside the Verdigris mark. Each bar is a left border.

A message that a script writes into the page goes into a status line, which a screen reader reads at its next pause. Only an error that appears with no field to move focus to uses role="alert", which interrupts. A message already in the page when it loads is plain text, since neither role announces it then.

text: The mark and the first word give each message its kind in a shape and in words, so color never carries it alone. A status line reaches a screen reader without moving focus or cutting off what it is reading, and keeping alerts for errors keeps interruptions rare.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1, 1.4.11 and 4.1.3; WAI-ARIA 1.2 status and alert roles

correct.caption: The parts of each message: its 24 px mark, its first word, its words, the 4 px bar on an error or a warning, and the Error Band behind an error on Newsprint.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 18.18. Three messages are told apart only by the color of their boxes, with no mark, no first word and no bar.

code.name: Messages
code.caption: An error, a warning and a success, live in both themes.

specs.value: None fits; WAI-ARIA 1.2’s status role, and its alert role for an error with no field.

specs.label: States
specs.value: Error, warning and success; inside a line of text, the 16 px marks.

specs.label: Keyboard
specs.value: None: a message takes no focus.

specs.value: None; its words are the message.

specs.value: No control.

rules.title: Say in words what is loading, and when nothing is there, say what is missing and what to do.
rule: While a part of the page waits for its data, it shows a still drawing and words that name what is coming, such as “Loading the tracker”, in a status line, with no spinner and no pulse (Rule 17.7). The words sit where the content will, so nothing jumps when the data lands.

When the data holds nothing, the part says what is missing and what to do next, inside a dashed edge: “No bills match these filters. Clear the filters to see every bill.” The empty words are plain text, and they name a step the reader can take on the page, such as a control in the filter bar.

text: Words tell every reader what is happening. A spinner shows only that something is happening, and a pulse moves without end. Saying what to do next turns an empty list into a step.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.2 and 4.1.3; design judgment

correct.caption: The parts of a loading state, its still drawing and its words, and of an empty state, its dashed edge, what is missing and what to do next.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 18.19. A spinning circle with no words stands for loading, and when nothing matches, the space is left blank.

code.name: Loading and empty states
code.caption: A loading state and an empty state, live in both themes.

specs.label: Pattern
specs.value: None fits; the status role for the loading words.

specs.label: States
specs.value: Loading: the words and a still drawing. Empty: what is missing and what to do, inside a dashed edge. Loaded: the content in the same place.

specs.label: Keyboard
specs.value: None of its own; the control the empty words name takes Tab.

specs.label: Accessible name
specs.value: None; the words say it.

specs.label: A screen reader hears
specs.value: The loading words once, at the next pause, when loading starts; the content when it lands; the empty words when the reader reaches them.

specs.label: Target
specs.value: Any control the empty words name, wherever the page holds it, at least 44 px tall.

specs.label: Forced colors
specs.value: The dashed edge and the drawing hold in CanvasText.

specs.label: Light and dark
specs.value: Loading and empty words in the secondary color, 5.49 to 1 on Newsprint and 7.26 on Charcoal.

specs.label: Motion
specs.value: None: the drawing is still, and nothing moves while the reader waits.

specs.label: Browser support
specs.value: ARIA states and roles are read by screen readers, and MDN’s data does not track which screen reader reads which; chapter 19 lists them as not tested here.

builders: Swap the loading words for the content in one write, and keep the box the same height while it waits.

rules.title: Update a live tracker in place, and say each change once in a status line.
rule: A tracker built from chapter 11’s marks is a list of steps, each with its name and one state word: Done, Now, You can take part now, Not yet, Never happened or Stopped (Rules 11.2 and 11.4). When a bill moves, the tracker redraws only the steps that changed and writes one sentence to its status line that names the new step, and the bill too where the page follows more than one.

The tracker takes no focus and moves nothing on the page when it updates. While its data loads it says so in words (Rule 18.19), and when nothing matches it says what to do. When the data fails it gives the error with its mark and how to try again, and a record that has gone unchecked carries the warning of Rule 11.10.

text: One polite sentence for each change lets a screen reader user hear what moved without losing their place, and redrawing only the changed steps keeps a sighted reader from losing theirs. The states stay in words, so an update never rests on a mark changing color.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1 and 4.1.3; WAI-ARIA 1.2 status role; Rule 11.5

correct.caption: The parts of a live tracker: the bill’s name, the six steps with their marks and state words, the status line under the list, and the check date with its warning mark.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 18.20. An “Updated!” box flashes up for three seconds and does not say which bill moved or where.

code.name: Tracker
code.caption: A tracker that updates, live. Each change is said once in the line under it.

specs.label: Pattern
specs.value: None fits; list markup for the steps and the status role for an update.

specs.label: States
specs.value: Done, Now, You can take part now, Not yet, Never happened and Stopped (Rules 11.2 and 11.4); loading; empty; error; the warning on a record unchecked too long (Rule 11.10).

specs.label: Keyboard
specs.value: None of its own; a link inside, such as a bill’s page, takes Tab.

specs.label: Accessible name
specs.value: The list’s label names the bill; each step its name and state word.

specs.label: A screen reader hears
specs.value: The steps read in order; on an update, one sentence from the status line, once.

specs.label: Target
specs.value: 44 px for any control on a tracker (Rule 11.7).

specs.label: Forced colors
specs.value: Chapter 11’s marks keep their shapes in CanvasText, and the words carry each state.

specs.label: Light and dark
specs.value: Chapter 11’s marks on Charcoal, in Newsprint and Dim Newsprint, with the take-part disc keeping its red.

specs.label: Browser support
specs.value: ARIA states and roles are read by screen readers, and MDN’s data does not track which screen reader reads which; chapter 19 lists them as not tested here.

builders: Write the sentence into a status line that was in the page, empty, from the start, and write only once for each bill that moves.

rules.title: Page through a report with buttons that keep their place and a status line that names each page.
rule: A report reader shows one page at a time, with Previous page and Next page buttons, each with its arrow beside its word, and the page’s size as a choice of Fit width or Full size (Rule 18.3). The status line names the page, the count and the page’s title, such as “Page 2 of 4:” and the title.

On the first page Previous page stays in place with aria-disabled and the line “This is the first page.”, and on the last Next page does the same; neither button moves focus. At Full size the page scrolls as Rule 18.11 sets. A page that is loading says so in the status line, and one that fails gives the error and how to try again. A reader that fills the screen opens in a native modal dialog.

text: Buttons that keep their place let a keyboard reader press Next page again and again without hunting for it, and a status line says where the reader is while focus stays put. A radio choice for the size says that only one size holds.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.3, 4.1.2 and 4.1.3; APG Button and Radio Group patterns; the APG Carousel pattern’s rule that its buttons do not move focus

correct.caption: The parts of a report reader: the page view, Previous page and Next page with their arrows, the unavailable button’s dashed edge and reason, the size choice, and the status line.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 18.21. On the last page Next page disappears, and focus falls back to the top of the page.

code.name: Report reader
code.caption: A four-page report, live. Press Next page until the last page: the button keeps focus and says why it waits.

specs.label: Pattern
specs.value: APG Button for each page button, in a named group with no toolbar role; APG Radio Group for the size; APG Dialog (Modal) for a reader that fills the screen.

specs.label: States
specs.value: First page, a middle page and the last page, each unavailable button with its reason; Fit width or Full size checked; loading; error. Hover. Focus.

specs.label: Keyboard
specs.value: Tab: the page while it scrolls, Previous page, Next page, then the size choice. Enter or Space turns the page. The arrow keys change the size.

specs.label: Accessible name
specs.value: “Previous page” and “Next page”; the size choice’s legend, such as “Page size”; the page by the report’s title.

specs.label: A screen reader hears
specs.value: After a press, the status line: the page, the count and the title. At either end, the disabled state and the reason.

specs.label: Target
specs.value: 44 px tall.

specs.label: Forced colors
specs.value: An unavailable button keeps its dashed edge, and the arrows draw in currentColor.

specs.label: Light and dark
specs.value: The page sits on --oa-color-field-ground, White on Newsprint and Prussian on Charcoal.

specs.label: Browser support
specs.value: <dialog> and showModal(): Chrome 37, Edge 79, Firefox 98, Safari 15.4, Safari on iOS 15.4. The dialog is needed only for a reader that fills the screen.

builders: Turn the page by swapping its content inside the same page view, and write the status line after the swap, so the line never names a page the reader cannot see yet.

rules.title: Step through a loop with Play, Reset the loop, Previous step and Next step, and say each step once.
rule: A loop stepper walks a reader through a loop of connections one step at a time. Its buttons run in one order in every product, Play, Reset the loop, Previous step and Next step, each with its utility icon beside its word (Rule 11.14). One polite live region says each step as it arrives, “Step 2 of 3:” and the step’s sentence, and the step list marks the current step with aria-current="step" and a 4 px bar.

Nothing plays until the reader presses Play. Play becomes Pause while it plays and Play again at the end, its icon and its word changing together, and it holds each step about 250 ms a word and never under six seconds, with reduced motion too (Rule 17.3). Next step, Previous step and Reset the loop stop the playback, and no button moves focus. At the start, Previous step and Reset the loop stay in place with aria-disabled and their reason; at the end, Next step does.

text: Play on request keeps the page still for a reader who did not ask it to move, and a pace set by the words gives a slow reader time to finish each step. Buttons that keep focus let a reader press Next step again and again, and one live region says each step without repeating the rest.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.1, 2.2.2, 4.1.2 and 4.1.3; APG Carousel pattern, its buttons without its slide roles

correct.caption: The parts of a loop stepper: Play with its icon and word, Reset the loop, Previous step, Next step, an unavailable button’s reason, the live line, and the step list with its current step’s 4 px bar.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 18.22. The loop starts on its own when the page loads, repeats without end and offers no button to pause it.

code.name: Loop stepper
code.caption: A three-step loop, live. Press Next step and listen for the line; press Play and it holds each step long enough to read.

specs.label: Pattern
specs.value: None fits. The Carousel pattern is nearest, and the stepper takes its buttons and its rule that no button moves focus, without its slide roles.

specs.label: States
specs.value: Ready; step 1, 2 or 3; playing, with Pause; paused; ended, with Play again; unavailable buttons with their reasons; the current step’s bar.

specs.label: Keyboard
specs.value: Tab through the four buttons; Enter or Space presses one; focus stays on the button pressed.

specs.label: Accessible name
specs.value: “Play”, “Pause” or “Play again”; “Reset the loop”; “Previous step”; “Next step”. Play changes its word, so it carries no pressed state.

specs.label: A screen reader hears
specs.value: Each step once, at the next pause: “Step 1 of 3:” and its sentence. The button’s new word when Play becomes Pause, while focus is on it.

specs.label: Target
specs.value: 44 px tall.

specs.label: Forced colors

specs.label: Light and dark

specs.label: Browser support

rules.title: Reach a drawing’s items from one Tab stop with the arrow keys, and give every drawing its words.
rule: The items in an atlas drawing, such as its areas, variables and loops, are toggle buttons in one group. The Tab key reaches the drawing once, at the selected item or the first, and the arrow keys move between items in reading order, with Home and End for the first and the last. Enter or Space selects an item, which lights its related items and opens its record in a panel, or a sheet on a phone; Escape closes it and returns focus to the item.

A readout line under the drawing repeats the name of the item in focus, so a reader who zooms in sees it without hovering. Each drawing also offers its lines in words behind a disclosure (Rule 18.8), and a drawing that holds values offers its data as a table the same way. Full size opens it in a native modal dialog. Zoom stays in words, as Zoom in, Zoom out, Fit and Reset.

text: One Tab stop for each drawing keeps a keyboard reader from passing every item to leave it, and the arrow keys still reach each one. The lines in words, with a table where a drawing holds values, give a reader who cannot see the drawing the same connections, and the readout takes the place of help that would show only on hover.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.1.1, 1.4.13, 2.1.1, 2.5.1 and 4.1.2; APG Button, Disclosure and Dialog (Modal) patterns

correct.caption: The parts of the diagram controls: the drawing’s items, the item in focus with its heavier mark and underlined label, the selected item, the muted items, the readout line, the panel with its title, and the disclosure for the lines in words.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 18.23. The drawing answers only to a pointer: the Tab key passes over it, and each item’s words show only in a box on hover.

specs.label: A screen reader hears

specs.label: Target

specs.value: Marks keep their shapes in CanvasText, and the selected item keeps its bold label.

specs.label: Light and dark

rules.title: Write a typed ID with its type in words, and make it a link only when it opens the record.
rule: A typed ID names a record in the atlas by its type and its code together, such as “Loop R10” or “Reform R-01”, so a reader never meets a bare code (chapter 02’s house rule H11). The chip sets both in the label style on a hairline edge, in the text’s ink, and color never codes its type.

A chip that opens its record is a link, underlined as Rule 18.5 sets, 1 px at rest and 2 px on hover, with a target at least 24 px tall; where the words around it do not name the record, the link’s description does. A chip that only names a record is plain text, with no role and no Tab stop.

text: The type in words tells every reader what the code refers to, where a color would leave a screen reader, or a reader who cannot see the color, with a bare code. A chip that takes focus only when it goes somewhere keeps the Tab order to things that act.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.3.1, 1.4.1 and 2.4.4; chapter 02, house rule H11

correct.caption: The parts of a typed ID chip: its type word, its code, the hairline edge, and as a link, its underline on hover and its 24 px target.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 18.24. The chips show bare codes, and only their fills say which is a loop and which is a reform.

code.name: Typed ID chip

specs.label: Pattern

specs.label: States

specs.label: Keyboard

specs.label: Accessible name

specs.label: A screen reader hears
specs.value: As text, its words; as a link, its words and its role.
